title: Is iron treatment beneficial in, iron-deficient but non-anaemic (IDNA) endurance athletes? A systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Burden RJ, Morton K, Richards T, Whyte GP, Pedlar CR
population: Iron-deficient non-anaemic endurance athletes in 17 studies
findings: 17 eligible studies pooled. Iron treatment had a large effect on serum ferritin (Hedges g = 1.088, 95% CI 0.914 to 1.263), serum iron (g = 1.004, 0.828 to 1.181) and transferrin saturation (g = 0.741, 0.564 to 0.919).
Moderate effect on haemoglobin concentration (g = 0.695, 95% CI 0.533 to 0.836) and VO2max (g = 0.610, 95% CI 0.399 to 0.821).
Regression showed a significant interaction between treatment duration and the ferritin effect; treatments beyond 80 days appeared to have the least effect on serum ferritin.
Authors conclude iron treatment improves iron status and aerobic capacity in iron-deficient non-anaemic endurance athletes.
limitations: Small heterogeneous studies and mixed regimens; abstract gives no sex-stratified results or risk-of-bias detail. Supports treatment only in documented deficiency under medical supervision.
implications: When a user logs low ferritin or a clinician-diagnosed deficiency, annotate fitness-test and threshold estimates as possibly suppressed and re-test after treatment (about 8-12 weeks, a design default consistent with the 80-day observation) instead of lowering long-term targets.
Do not recommend iron supplementation in-app; recommend medical testing and treatment.

verification.notes: Crossref matches (BJSM, online 2014-10; issue year 2015). Numbers confirmed in Europe PMC abstract (PMID 25361786). Evidence level lowered A to B for small heterogeneous trials.
